### 14.10 — the sweep was measuring its own patience, and 1440 was mostly innocent

- [x] **DONE 2026-10-06 (the retry, below) — Five runs of `sweep-widths.mjs` on the afternoon of 2026-09-20, same
  account, same dev server, same seed.** 1440 truncated the guided tour to one
  block three times, walked all 33 steps once, and on the fifth **aborted the
  whole width after 84 of 125 surfaces** on `locator.click: Timeout 15000ms
  exceeded`. 392 and 320 did neither, in any of the five.
  **This is its own item because it is an instrument problem, not an inventory
  one.** Andrew, 2026-09-20: *"Folding it into the inventory work would bury a
  flaky instrument inside a finished item, and then every future 1440 result
  carries an asterisk nobody can see."*
  **Two symptoms, and whether they are one fault is unknown.** A tour that
  stops after its first tab and a width that dies on a click may share a cause
  — a click that silently misses, a tab that never finishes arriving — or may
  be unrelated. Nothing measured so far distinguishes them, and guessing is
  the tempting move.
  **The cheapest experiment is a run that does nothing else:** open the tour at
  1440 twenty times, record how many blocks it reaches each time, and take a
  screenshot of the frame where it stops. Twenty runs of one tour is a few
  minutes; a full sweep is nine.
  **Two detectors already watch for this and neither can close it.** The
  cross-width check fails whenever the tour's tab count differs by width, but
  deliberately refuses to say which width is wrong. The ledger
  (`receipts/sweep-widths-ledger.json`) counts aborts and shortfalls per width
  and fails when more than two of the last five runs did not complete — so the
  pattern becomes visible on its own, but neither one explains it.
  **Note that the ledger records 1440 as `complete` while its tour truncates**,
  because the truncated steps are accounted for as declared skips. That is
  correct and worth knowing: the two detectors answer different questions and
  only one of them is about this fault.
  **THE TWENTY-RUN EXPERIMENT IS DONE, AND THIS IS A DIFFERENT ITEM FROM THE
  ONE ABOVE — 2026-09-20, `node scripts/tour-runs.mjs 20 1440 392`.** Twenty
  cold opens of the tour at 1440, with five control runs at 392 in the same
  batch. The control completed 5/5, so the walk works and what 1440 did is
  about 1440.

  | at 1440 | runs |
  |---|---|
  | 34 steps, six blocks `5+6+6+5+6+6`, complete | **16** |
  | 31 steps, six blocks, complete | 1 |
  | 29 steps, **five** blocks — the first block never happened | 1 |
  | 11 steps, two blocks | 1 |
  | 0 steps — the card never arrived | 1 |

  **17 of 20 complete. It is not "the tour dies after its first tab."** That
  framing came from three sweep runs and no run here reproduced it. The real
  rate is roughly one in seven, and it has at least three different shapes.

  **AND THERE IS A SIGNATURE, WHICH IS THE USEFUL PART.** Both early deaths
  show a block opening on a total lower than its real one and then correcting:
  `1/5 2/5 3/5 4/5 5/5 1/3 2/6 3/6 …` — the second block announced three steps
  and had six. **2 of 20 runs grew a plan mid-block, and both of them died.
  All 17 runs without that growth completed. The 392 control grew none.**
  `Walkthrough.jsx` already documents this exact hazard beside the code that
  is supposed to prevent it — the count is meant to be taken once the screen
  has stopped arriving — so the guard exists and is incomplete at 1440.

  **WHAT IS STILL UNEXPLAINED, AND IT IS NOT THE SAME THING.** The sweep
  reports 1440 at `1 block declaring 5 = 5 steps` **consistently**, not one
  time in seven. The sweep reaches the tour after roughly eighty surfaces of
  clicking, sheets and tab switches; this script goes straight to it on a cold
  sign-in. So the sweep's truncation is a different phenomenon from the
  intermittent one measured here, and the next probe is the sweep's own tempo:
  `settle()` returns after 130ms of quiet where this script waits a flat
  second, and `TOUR_WAIT` exists on `tour-runs.mjs` to repeat these twenty runs
  at that pace.

  **THE TEMPO ARM SETTLED IT, AND THE ANSWER IS THE INSTRUMENT — 2026-09-20,
  `TOUR_WAIT=300 node scripts/tour-runs.mjs 20 1440 392`.** The same twenty
  runs, pressing *Next* 300ms after each card instead of a flat second,
  because `settle()` returns after 130ms of quiet and that is the tempo the
  sweep actually presses at:

  | arm | result |
  |---|---|
  | 1440px at 300ms, 20 runs | **20 of 20 stopped at exactly 5 steps, one block `[5]`** |
  | 392px at 1000ms, 5 control runs | 5 of 5 complete, 33 steps, six blocks |
  | 392px at 300ms, 5 runs | **0 of 5 complete**, four of them dying at 4 steps |

  **That is the sweep's own line, reproduced twenty times out of twenty:**
  `tour · the blocks  1 block(s) declaring 5 = 5 step(s); 5 walked`. And the
  short wait ends the tour at 392 as well — at 4 steps rather than 5, which is
  exactly the size of that width's first block. **The tour dies on the press
  that has to carry it to the next TAB, whenever that press comes too soon.**
  It is not a property of 1440; 1440 is simply where the sweep's timing
  happened to land.

  **SO THE ITEM SPLITS, AND THE LARGER HALF IS OURS.**

  - **The sweep's consistent truncation is the sweep.** It has been measuring
    its own patience. `settle()` is a cap on a repaint and the next block's
    card is not a repaint of this one — the fix is to wait for the next card
    to exist rather than for the page to go quiet. **Not done here: this
    session was asked to run the experiment and stop.** No sweep result about
    the tour above step 5 at 1440 was ever a fact about the product.
  - ~~**The cold-open failures are real and rare.** 2 of 20 at a full second
    between presses, both carrying the plan-growth signature — a block opening
    on a total lower than its real one, `1/3` then `2/6`. That is the product
    and it is worth fixing.~~ **STRUCK 2026-09-20. THE 2-IN-20 WAS NEVER A
    FACT ABOUT THE PRODUCT AND MUST NOT BE QUOTED AGAIN** — it was quoted
    twice in one day before it was caught.

    **The fault was the same one the sweep had, one size smaller: a card
    absent at the moment of looking was read as the tour ending.**
    `tour-runs.mjs` pressed, waited a flat second, then asked whether the
    card had gone — and a tour crossing into its next tab has no card for a
    few hundred milliseconds. Nothing about the product was being measured at
    that instant. The same script waiting for the next card to EXIST saw
    **0 of 20** short at 1440, all twenty walking the full 34 steps.

    **What that does and does not establish, because the difference is the
    whole lesson of this item.** It voids the evidence; it does not acquit the
    product. 0 of 20 cannot prove a clean walk — if the real rate were one in
    ten, twenty runs would come back empty about one time in eight. So the
    honest statement is **there is no longer any measurement suggesting a
    cold-open failure exists**, not that one has been ruled out. The
    plan-growth signature itself is also no longer fatal by construction: a
    block whose total changes mid-flight produces a CHANGED step counter,
    which is exactly what `nextCard()` treats as the next card arriving.
    **Anyone re-opening this needs a new measurement, not this number.**

  **AND NOW IT IS MEASURED IN THE SWEEP ITSELF RATHER THAN BY PROXY —
  2026-09-20, second session.** Everything above rests on one number nobody
  had ever read: *300ms* was chosen because `settle()` returns after 130ms of
  quiet. That is an inference about a line of code, not a reading of it.
  `settle()` RETURNS the milliseconds it waited and the tour walk was throwing
  that value away, so the load-bearing figure in the finding was the one
  figure never measured. It now prints — `tour · the pace`.

  **The reproduction argument was also weaker than it read.** At 1440 the
  blocks are `5+6+6+5+6+6`, so *any* death on the first tab-crossing press
  produces "5 steps, one block". Twenty out of twenty matching the sweep's
  line confirms that a tab-crossing press can be killed; on its own it does
  not confirm that TEMPO is what kills it in the sweep. Four runs of the real
  sweep at 1440 close that gap directly:

  | run | what changed | `settle()` returned | result |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | default | nothing | `223 275 260 255` **`583`** | 5 steps, 1 block |
  | canary, cap 1ms | `SWEEP_TOUR_SETTLE=1` | `21 21 22 26 21` | 5 steps, 1 block |
  | held | `SWEEP_TOUR_HOLD=1000` | same ~250, plus a 1s hold | **34 steps, 6 blocks, every one clean** |

  **The sweep's real tempo at 1440 is ~250ms, not 300ms** — 223–281ms on an
  in-tab press and 528–630ms on the press that crosses to a new tab. Holding
  a further second between presses, and changing nothing else, walks the
  whole tour. **The truncation is the sweep's patience, proved inside the
  sweep.** Reproduced three times; the clean one is 17:19:30, the other two
  carried a concurrent `app/src` edit and say so.

  **AND THE CAP IS NOT THE CEILING PEOPLE THINK IT IS.** On the held run
  `settle()` came back at `1007`, `1019` and `1001` — it hit its own 1000ms
  cap at three of the five tab crossings. So even "wait for quiet, up to a
  second" is not enough there. This is the documented
  *`settle()` cannot catch an animation that has not started yet* one level
  up: it cannot catch a CARD that has not been created yet.

  **ONE HYPOTHESIS TESTED AND KILLED, WHICH IS WHY IT IS WRITTEN DOWN.** The
  sweep trails `1/4 2/5 3/5 4/5 5/5` where the 300ms script trails
  `1/5 2/5 …` — the sweep reads the first card declaring FOUR and it corrects
  to five, which is the plan-growth signature the cold-open deaths carry. It
  looked like a second cause hiding under an identical summary line. It is
  not: the `1/4` appears in all four sweep runs **including both that walked
  the full 34 steps**, so growth on card 1 is survivable and is only the
  sweep reading the plan a beat earlier than the other script does.

  **THE CONSEQUENCE NOBODY HAD NAMED: the 1440 baseline is a record of the
  fault.** `sweep-widths.expected.json` lists `tour · step 1`–`7` at 1440 and
  1–33 elsewhere. The default run truncating at 5 **passed** the expected-count
  gate and exited 0; the held run walking the real 34 **failed** it with 27
  `NOT EXPECTED`. So at 1440 the gate has been grading the product against an
  instrument fault, and the answer it holds as correct is the broken one.
  **Do not `--write-expected` to clear this** — that writes a hold-dependent
  run in as the truth. It is fixed by fixing the walk.

  **RE-ESTABLISHED ON A STABLE TREE, AND FIVE RUNS THROWN AWAY TO DO IT —
  2026-09-20, at `c4058d3`.** The five runs above were taken between 10:07 and
  10:25 while another session was editing `app/src`; its commit landed at
  10:30:35. **Two of the five were caught mid-edit by the sweep's own
  source-change guard, and the other three simply predate the change** — so
  all five were discarded rather than averaged with what came after. A rate
  computed across two versions of the page is the same lie as a receipt that
  cannot tell stale from failed. Everything below is one tree, zero
  source-change warnings, both canaries caught.

  | arm | result |
  |---|---|
  | `TOUR_WAIT=250`, 20 runs at 1440 | **20 of 20 at 5 steps, one block `[5]`** |
  | control, 5 runs at 392 @1000ms | 5 of 5 complete, 33 steps, six blocks |
  | tempo arm, 5 runs at 392 @250ms | **0 of 5**, stopping at 4, 10, 4, 10, 4 |
  | sweep at 1440, default | pace `273 257 248 251` **`562`** — 5 steps, one block |
  | sweep at 1440, `SWEEP_TOUR_HOLD=1000` | **34 steps, six blocks**, caps of `1019`, `1007`, `1023` at the crossings |

  **250ms is the measured tempo, not the 300ms stand-in**, and it reproduces
  everything the stand-in did. The tempo arm is the load-bearing one: the same
  short wait kills the tour at 392 too, so the subject column is about pressing
  fast and not about 1440.

  **AND HERE IS THE PART THAT IS WORSE THAN A CAVEAT.** The truncated run does
  not merely fail to measure steps 6 and 7 — **it declares them unreachable**:

  ```
  tour · step @1440   5 step(s), ended on the last card it had (5 of 5)
                      — 2 inventory label(s) this dashboard cannot produce:
                        tour · step 6, tour · step 7
  ```

  A declared skip in this repo is supposed to be *a surface proved
  unreachable*. Here it is asserted off the back of a walk that died, so the
  sweep **manufactures the justification for its own fault, once per run**, and
  that is why the default run exits 0 and passes the expected-count gate. It is
  not that the baseline happens to record seven steps; it is that the
  instrument re-certifies the truncation as correct every time it runs. Any
  fix has to make that skip provable or stop it being issued.

  **Done when:** the sweep waits for the next card instead of for quiet, and a
  clean twenty-run batch at that tempo shows the tour reaching six blocks at
  1440 — **and** `tour · step 6`/`7` are no longer issued as declared skips at
  1440 — **and** `sweep-widths.expected.json` carries `tour · step 1`–`34` at
  1440 as a consequence of that walk rather than of a `SWEEP_TOUR_HOLD` run —
  **and**, separately, the plan-growth signature is closed **deterministically
  rather than statistically**: the cold-open condition is forced on purpose, the
  tour still reaches six blocks under it, and the mechanism that was failing is
  named in `Walkthrough.jsx`.

### 14.11 — a check with a sanctioned word for testing nothing — DONE 2026-10-06

- [x] **A declared skip in this repo is supposed to mean a surface proved
  unreachable, and one of them is really just a walk that died — so the
  instrument certifies its own fault as correct on every run and the gate
  believes it. That is the disease at the level above the disease: not a check
  that tests nothing, but a check that has a sanctioned word for testing
  nothing.** Andrew's manager, 2026-09-20, on the finding in 14.10.
  **Split out of 14.10 deliberately and it is the larger item.** 14.10 is one
  instrument pressing too fast. This is about what the repo is allowed to call
  a skip, and it reaches every check that has ever declared one.

  **THE INSTANCE, SO THE RULE HAS SOMETHING TO STAND ON.** The width sweep's
  tour walk ended at step 5 at 1440 and printed:

  ```
  tour · step @1440   5 step(s), ended on the last card it had (5 of 5)
                      — 2 inventory label(s) this dashboard cannot produce:
                        tour · step 6, tour · step 7
  ```

  *This dashboard cannot produce* is a claim about the **product**. It rested
  entirely on `last.at === last.of` — the walk ended on the last card of a
  block. **At a tab boundary that is exactly what a walk that died looks
  like**, because the card there reads `5 of 5` too. So the run wrote its own
  truncation off as a property of the dashboard, once per run, and that is why
  the truncating run **exits 0 and passes the expected-count gate** while the
  complete walk fails it.

  **AND THE PART THAT MAKES IT AN ITEM RATHER THAN A BUG: THIS REPO ALREADY
  HAD THE RULE, AND THIS SITE WENT AROUND IT.** `sweep-widths.mjs` has exactly
  two places that issue a skip. One is `declareSkip(label, reason, reachable)`,
  which **re-asks a probe and refuses the skip if the surface is actually
  there** — its own comment says *"the run proves the surface was genuinely
  out of reach rather than taking the caller's word for it"*, and a refusal is
  louder than the thing it hid. The other is a bare `SKIPPED.push` in the walk
  accounting, with no probe and no way to refuse. **The correct pattern was
  forty lines away and had been for days.** Same shape as the animation fix
  that lived in `screenreader-structure.mjs` while the script measuring nothing
  but edges went without: a technique that lives in one instrument is not a
  technique the repo has.

  **THE RULE, WHICH IS THE DELIVERABLE.** A skip carries the evidence that the
  surface was **reached and refused**, or it is not a skip and the run does not
  get to pass on it. Anything that cannot produce that evidence stops being
  issued as a skip at all and becomes a finding. Three consequences worth
  writing separately:

  - **The evidence is an ACT, not a state.** `declareSkip` probes. The walk's
    evidence is that it pressed, waited the full bound, and nothing came.
    "The thing was not there when I looked" is not evidence — it is the
    sentence every dead walk also produces.
  - **A skip that cannot be refused is not a skip.** If no probe could ever
    contradict it, it is an assertion wearing a measurement's clothes.
  - **A run may not grade itself on skips it issued.** The truncating run
    passing its own gate is the whole failure in one line.

  **DONE ON THE INSTANCE, 2026-09-20.** `nextCard()` replaces the
  wait-for-quiet in both the tour walk and the four tab guides, and
  `endProved` is set only by a press whose full wait came back empty. A walk
  that stopped because the card was already gone writes **nothing** off and
  prints `ENDED WITHOUT PROOF` with the labels it refused to excuse.
  `SWEEP_TOUR_HOLD` is deleted in the same change — a switch that can make a
  check complete when the check cannot is one somebody reaches for on a bad
  afternoon.

  direction: a skip leaves **no** receipt, a crash leaves the **previous
  run's PASS** sitting on disk as the record of a run that never happened.
  **A stale green is worse than a missing one**, and this row reads as though
  the question were settled for all ten.

  bill, not a way in.** The guard is written with that stated in the function
  itself, so nobody reading it in six months mistakes it for a closed
  vulnerability and back-dates an incident that never happened.

## Release gates

From A1 § 11. Use these rather than "the wave is finished".

- **Gate A — safe private pilot.** Waves 1–4 closed or explicitly risk-accepted
  with a temporary safeguard. Every example CTA passes an automated mapping
  check. One complete booking lifecycle passes. Real-device phone pass done.
  External booking and email-failure alerts work.
- **Gate B — Andrew runs in parallel.** Money reconciles against his old
  records. Confirm/undo and audit history work. Daily export and fallback
  available. Ten real jobs complete with no lost state and no invisible missed
  message.
- **Gate C — Andrew retires the old system.** Several weeks of parallel
  operation reconcile. Restore drill passes. Weak-signal and retry pass.
  Cancellation/reschedule/quote/receipt lifecycle passes. He can recover
  tomorrow's schedule during an outage.
- **Gate D — sell to strangers.** Waves 1–8 closed. Legal pages match reality.
  `/examples` and pricing communicate without help. Admin spots failures before
  customers report them. A small group of pilot detailers has completed real
  jobs and their support failures have been addressed.

## Andrew's decisions — 2026-09-16, second round

**3.2 email cap — DEFERRED, and the audits' premise was wrong.** Andrew has
sent 100+ emails in a day with no failure, so the cap is not the hard wall A2
described. He is not paying ~$60 until there are customers, expected around
**December 2026**. Revisit then, not before.

**3.3 texting — ONE platform number, not one per detailer.** His words: *"I
don't need a text message for every single detailer to have their own separate
messaging software… the same with the phone number."* Exactly how Resend works
today — the platform sends, from the platform's identity, on the detailer's
behalf. **This is much cheaper and simpler than per-tenant numbers** and it
removes per-detailer A2P registration entirely.
**Provider, researched 2026-09-16:** **Telnyx at $0.0040/SMS** is the cheapest
credible option — about half Twilio's $0.0083, and Twilio's real cost is nearer
$0.011–0.013 once carrier surcharges land. **Plivo at $0.0055** is second and
mirrors Twilio's API if migration ever matters. **Recommendation: Telnyx.**
US A2P 10DLC registration is required either way — one registration, one
number, one brand. At a few hundred reminders a month this is **under $5/month**.
*Sources: [APIScout Twilio vs Plivo vs Telnyx 2026](https://apiscout.dev/guides/twilio-vs-plivo-vs-telnyx-sms-voice-api-2026), [Sinch SMS API comparison](https://sinch.com/blog/the-best-sms-api/).*

**8.2 phone testing — he has an iPhone 15 Pro Max and nothing else.** He asked
how real teams test phones they do not own. **That research is not done yet and
is now a task** — see 8.6. Do it before planning the mobile wave.

then just edit them. Then we shouldn't need a lawyer."* Accepted. 7.7 and 7.8
stay as written and the template work folds into them. **A business entity is

  automatic branch deploys still listed as *“worth doing”*. **If the repo is not
  connected, deploy previews do not exist**, and four documents recommend a
  mechanism a fifth says may be absent. Settling it is a 30-second look at
  Netlify's settings and Netlify is Andrew's. **The Wi-Fi route was chosen partly
  because it needs none of that confirmed.**

  **WHAT THE METHOD SAYS IT CANNOT DO, in its own words:** nothing about Android
  until somebody lends a phone; nothing about older or smaller iPhones, and a
  6.7" screen **hides** thumb-reach problems a 5.4" one shows; and nothing
  repeatable — a human pass finds things, it does not guard them, so anything it
  finds should become a check.

  **HONESTLY LABELLED: the Wi-Fi route is UNVERIFIED by this session**, which had
  no dev server by instruction. The two things that can break it are named in the
  method (the PC firewall on port 5173, and Vite needing `--host`), both
  one-time.

## Adopting the operating-system report

`docs/operating-system-report-2026-09-16.md` is the research Andrew commissioned.
**Its headline finding independently matches what this repo already knew**: the
root problem is that a check can print "clean" having tested nothing, which
makes every other process unsafe. It calls the fix **proof-carrying work** — no
green verdict without a machine-readable receipt showing targets discovered,
attempted, completed, assertions run, skips, and a deliberately broken canary
that had to fail.

**Do not adopt the whole report at once.** Its own § 6 says so, and this repo's
history of accreting process is exactly what that warning is about. Its
week-one sequence, which supersedes starting at Wave 1 of this file:

1. [x] **DONE 2026-09-16.** Tag the repo before any prune
   (`pre-doc-prune-2026-09-16`). Annotated tag on `2a10b86`, carrying the
   command to recover any pruned document: `git show
   pre-doc-prune-2026-09-16:docs/<path>`. Verified with `git tag -l -n1`.

   `scripts/receipt.mjs` — one file, no new dependency, because the rules that
   matter are arithmetic *between* fields (expected = discovered = attempted =
   completed) and no JSON Schema vocabulary says that without a custom keyword.
   **It never trusts the `status` a check wrote; it recomputes the verdict.**
   `node scripts/receipt.mjs` validates every receipt in `receipts/`.
   **Verified by breaking it on purpose.** `tests/receipt.test.mjs` is 13 cases,
   one per rule, each a receipt that breaks that rule and nothing else — 13/13
   pass. Then three rules were disabled in the validator (the canary rule, the

   **THE FIRST CERTIFICATION ATTEMPT WAS WORTHLESS AND LOOKED FINE.**
   `--break=leak` and `--break=sentinel` both PASSED, because a table with
   `using (true)` trips several detectors at once and "the canary was caught"
   was true no matter which one was switched off. **A negative control that
   can be caught by the wrong detector certifies nothing.** Every finding now

   `leak` specifically.

   `platform_admin_events` carries a `business_id` AND zero policies on

   **The second was a wrong finding I published and then withdrew an hour
   later, and it is the more useful of the two.** I reported that
   `connected_accounts` had a policy that could never fire because
   `authenticated` held no grant. **False.**
   `20260908001000_connected_accounts.sql` revokes the table and grants the
   columns back **one at a time**, withholding `connect_state` on purpose —
   *"a value nobody can read is a value nobody can leak."*
   `has_table_privilege` answers **false** for a column-granted table, so the
   matrix asked for `select=*`, was refused **for the columns rather than the
   rows**, and I read a column refusal as a row denial. **The two are
   indistinguishable from outside.** It uses `has_column_privilege` per column
   now and asks each table for exactly what a browser may have;
   `connected_accounts` then passes like any other table. FOUND.md carries
   the withdrawal.

   **A browser reads a table only if the role holds a grant — possibly per
   column — AND a policy lets the row through.** Keying on either alone is
   wrong, in opposite directions, one table each.

   erases if nobody writes it down.

   **THE SECOND CANARY IS A DEFINER FUNCTION THAT TRUSTS ITS CALLER'S TENANT

   **THREE DEFECTS IN THE CHECK, EVERY ONE FOUND BY THE CANARY REFUSING TO BE
   CAUGHT. Each is now a `docs/gotchas.md` entry:**

   - **PostgREST caches its schema.** The freshly created canary answered
     `404 PGRST202`, and a 404 reads exactly like an empty, correct denial. It
     issues `notify pgrst, 'reload schema'`, waits, and then **probes the
     canary for reachability** — an unreachable canary now says so instead of
     reporting a missed one. Those are opposite diagnoses: one means the
     detector is blind, the other means the run proved nothing.
   - **`create function` grants EXECUTE to PUBLIC**, so the canary was
     anon-callable too. The rule was *"an actor of A must not get more than an
     anonymous stranger"*; anon got B's rows as well, so A was getting no
     more, and **the canary came back clean while visibly returning the secret
     it was leaking**. A comparative assertion is blind exactly where both
     sides fail together. The matrix now also refuses any function handing a
     tenant's own text to an anonymous caller, against a **three-name
     allowlist with written reasons** — `--break=allowlist` empties it and all
     three become findings, which is the proof it is refusable rather than
     decorative.
   - **`get_public_business_profile_by_host` was reported `ok` having resolved
     nothing.** The fixture domain carried no `verified_at`, and both host
     endpoints filter on `d.verified_at is not null`. A fixture that cannot be
     found is a target that was never tested — the missing-recipe failure
     arriving through the argument instead of the table.

   **Five sabotages, all refused:** `--break=canary`, `--break=leak`,
   `--break=rpc`, `--break=allowlist`, `--break=recipe`. Both canaries and
   both fixture tenants verified gone afterwards, `demo-detail` untouched.

   **No leak was found in any of the 38 tenant-owned tables**, by any of the
   four actors, on read, update, delete or forged-tenancy insert.

   **EXTENDED TO STORAGE AND REALTIME, 2026-09-20 — the last two of the four
   boundaries, and step 6 is now complete.** **PASS — 77 targets, 729
   assertions, 0 failures, FOUR canaries, each caught by its own detector.**

   **WHY IT WAS NOT ALREADY FINISHED, IN ONE SENTENCE ABOUT ONE TABLE.**
   `job_photos` passed above — every actor of A refused every one of B's photo
   rows, by four detectors. **The photographs were never fetched once.** The
   row holds a `path`; the bytes live in a bucket behind a policy on
   `storage.objects` in another schema that nothing in the table matrix reads.
   A green `job_photos` reads as coverage of job photos and is coverage of
   job-photo metadata.

   **6 · STORAGE.** Buckets are discovered from `storage.buckets`, not named,
   for the same reason tables are. Three buckets each run — `business-media`,
   `job-photos` and the canary. The invariant is the RPC section's word for
   word: **an actor of A must not get more out of B's folder than an anonymous
   stranger gets.** That handles `business-media` correctly without
   special-casing it — a tenant's logo is served to the whole internet on
   purpose, so A seeing it is the product and A seeing what anon cannot is the
   defect. Per bucket: download B's file, list B's folder, list A's folder as a
   removed member, upload into B's folder, delete B's file, and confirm A can
   still reach its own. **No leak in either real bucket.**

   **THE CANARY IS A BUCKET WHOSE POLICY SCOPES TO THE BUCKET AND NOTHING
   ELSE** — the 1am mistake, where every real policy here scopes to the first
   folder segment, which is the owning business's id. Caught by
   `[storage-read]` specifically, which is the detector that proves the BYTES
   crossed rather than that a request was allowed.

   **7 · REALTIME, WHICH IS THREE MECHANISMS WEARING ONE NAME.** The
   publication decides what streams at all; RLS decides who receives it;
   and broadcast/presence is guarded by something else entirely. Asking it as
   one question covers at most a third.

   - **7a, the publication.** Zero tenant-owned tables are published, so
     nothing streams to anybody. The canary table is published on purpose, or
     that line would print identically with the query broken.
   - **7b, delivery.** **Not certified, and said plainly.** The canary table,
     published with `using (true)`, granted, `replica identity full`, owner A
     `SUBSCRIBED`, `realtime.subscription` carrying the row server-side, slot
     active, row inserted — **nothing arrived, three runs, cold slot, 15s
     each.** `postgres_changes` does not deliver on this project. An empty
     array is also what perfect isolation looks like, so the probe proves its
     own socket first by sending itself a broadcast and hearing it back; it
     did. The verdict prints `NOT DELIVERING — detector uncertified`, rides in
     `warnings`, and `realtime-stream` is **deliberately left out of the
     receipt's canary gate**. Uncovered, not clean. Nothing is exposed today —
     nothing tenant-owned is published and the app opens zero channels — but
     the day a table is published this must be re-proved first.
   - **7c, channels. THE ONE REAL FINDING OF THE NIGHT, and it is a standing
     risk rather than a live defect.** A channel opened **without**
     `private: true` is authorised by **nothing at all**. Proved by having a
     client with only the anon key and no session join a plain channel and
     receive a signed-in user's broadcast verbatim, sentinel and all. The app
     opens zero channels, so nothing leaks today. **The first
     `supabase.channel('bookings-' + businessId)` anybody writes is a
     cross-tenant channel on the day it ships**, because a business id is a
     guess away. Carried as a warning on every receipt so it cannot quietly
     stop being said. Private channels **are** closed: `realtime.messages` is
     RLS-on with zero policies and anon was refused in the same run.

   **SIX SABOTAGES, ALL REFUSED BY `receipt.mjs`, AND TWO OF THEM ARE THE ONLY
   ONES THAT PROVE ANYTHING.** `--break=storage`, `--break=realtime` and
   `--break=bucket-allowlist` are blunt: the storage canary trips three
   detectors, so silencing all three proves the canary can be missed and
   nothing about *which* detector the gate is on. That is the exact trap the
   RPC canary sprang on the first pass. So:

   - `--break=storage-read` silences **only** the byte comparison ->
     `CANARY NOT CAUGHT BY THE STORAGE-READ DETECTOR`, although `storage-list`
     and `storage-former` still trip on it.
   - `--break=realtime-pub` silences **only** the publication detector -> the
     run fails, although `[realtime-broadcast]` is caught.
   - `--break=bucket-allowlist` -> `business-media` reports as a
     `[storage-public]` finding, which is the proof the one-name allowlist is
     refusable rather than decorative.

   **A switch that turns off a whole section is a smoke test. A switch that
   turns off one detector is a certification.**

   **`min_assertions` RAISED 300 -> 700.** At 300, sections 6 and 7 could be
   deleted from the file entirely and the receipt would still pass its own
   assertion rule, because tables and RPCs alone run 693. A floor nobody raises
   is a floor that stops working.

   **TWO THINGS LEARNED THE HARD WAY, BOTH NOW IN `docs/gotchas.md`:** storage
   answers `200 []` for "denied" and for "nothing there", so every list is
   paired with a service-role count of what is actually in the folder; and
   running two copies of this script at once destroys each other's canaries
   and reads exactly like a blind detector. The teardown held through that
   collision — both canaries, the canary bucket, the publication entry, every
   planted object and both fixture tenants verified gone afterwards.

   **SELF-REPORTED, SAME AS ABOVE.** Every number here came from runs made by
   the session that wrote the check, against `kguqylyzgyzfktkfnhjb`. Not
   independently verified.

7. [~] **HALF DONE 2026-09-20. The prune is finished; the roadmap
   restructure is held.**

   **THE PRUNE — DONE.** `docs/archive/` is gone: 9 files, about 45,000 words,
   whose only remaining purpose was to be searched by a session that should be
   reading git history. **Nothing was deleted until the tag was proved to hold

   `pre-doc-prune-2026-09-16`, and two were recovered in full as a rehearsal —
   the old rulebook at 19,861 words and a retired session brief at 3,911.

   **AND THE FIRST COMPARISON SAID FIVE OF THE NINE DIFFERED FROM THE TAG**,
   which would have meant the safety net did not hold what it claimed. It was
   the instrument: the working copies are CRLF and git's blobs are LF, so a
   checksum over the raw bytes reports a difference that is not there. Once
   carriage returns were stripped, **all nine were identical and no commit had
   touched `docs/archive/` since the tag**. Worth knowing before somebody
   checksums a file against a git blob again.

   **Two live pointers were rewritten rather than left dangling** — `CLAUDE.md`
   named the old rulebook and this file named the old roadmap. Both now carry
   the `git show` command instead of a path.

   **WHAT WAS NOT PRUNED, AND WHY.** 38 documents outside `docs/archive/` have
   no inbound reference from anywhere. **They were left alone.** Most are
   design renderings and tenant-site explorations, which exist to be LOOKED AT
   rather than searched — the criterion for pruning does not fit them. And one
   candidate proved the point: `docs/the-deploy-is-not-the-push-2026-09-08.md`
   is unreferenced and is **directly relevant to 0.6**, carrying a correction
   whose own note says *"the reasoning is the lesson"*. Deleting it on a
   reference count would have destroyed exactly the thing tonight needed.
   Per-file judgement, not a bulk rule, and not tonight.

   **THE RESTRUCTURE — HELD, and written up instead:**
   `docs/roadmap-restructure-proposal.md`. What the structure would be, what it
   buys, what it costs, what would break, and the conditions it should be done
   under. **The reason it is held is not nerve:** this is the one file both
   sessions write to, it was edited by both of them repeatedly today, and **a
   tag cannot protect a file from being concurrently rewritten** — it can only
   return a version, and what a concurrent rewrite loses is nobody's version.
   One session, a quiet tree, a fresh tag, one pass. **Andrew rules on it.**

### 14.14 — ~~`tests/receipt-fields.test.mjs` is FAILING at committed HEAD~~ DONE 2026-09-24. The ENDPOINT was right and the TEST was stale

- [x] **DONE 2026-09-24. Found by DP Cowork on 2026-09-23 and reproduced independently before
  being written down.** The booking-receipt endpoint returns **32** columns
  where the test expects **31**. **The extra one is `address_source`**, added
  by **2.8**.

  **The measurement, from a run rather than from a reading:**

  ```
  48 passed, 3 failed, 51 assertions
  FAIL  the endpoint's list matches this file's, name for name and in order
        endpoint has 32, this file expects 31: only there [address_source], only here []
  FAIL  d7a79912 — the reply carries nothing outside the list sent as well: address_source
  FAIL  554722f5 — the reply carries nothing outside the list sent as well: address_source
  ```

  **One cause, three failures.** The list comparison fails once; the
  per-booking assertion fails once for each of the two bookings it walks. **A
  reader counting three failures will look for three problems.**

  **NOT FIXED HERE ON PURPOSE.** `address_source` is 2.8's column and 2.8's
  tree belongs to another session. **Fixing this means adding one name to the
  expected list** — but doing that from outside 2.8 would be deciding, on
  2.8's behalf, that the column is meant to be in the receipt's public reply.
  **That is a question about what a customer's receipt should disclose, not a
  test that needs quietening.**

  **Done when:** whoever owns 2.8 either adds `address_source` to the expected
  list, having said why a customer-facing receipt should carry how an address
  was arrived at — or removes it from the endpoint's reply. **Either way the
  answer goes in the commit, because a test edited to match an endpoint is the
  cheapest way in this repo to make a real disclosure change invisible.**

  **Why this is its own item:** it fails at committed `HEAD`, on `main`, right
  now. **Anything that runs the full battery sees a red and has no file to
  read about it** — and CLAUDE.md already warns that a red in a full run is a
  lead rather than a verdict, which is exactly the instruction that would
  cause somebody to dismiss this one.

  ---

  #### RESOLVED 2026-09-24. WHICH SIDE WAS WRONG WAS ESTABLISHED FIRST.

  **In one sentence: the endpoint is right and the test's list was stale, so the
  list was updated — and given a reason, so it cannot be updated that way again
  without one.**

  **INHERITED, NOT CAUSED, and it matters to whoever reads `git log`.** This was
  red at committed `HEAD` before either session on 2026-09-23 touched anything —
  confirmed then by `git stash -u` and a re-run producing the same 12 passed /
  1 failed, and confirmed again from source on 2026-09-24 before any edit this
  round. **Nothing in this repo's recent history broke it.** It was introduced
  by ROADMAP 2.8 adding `address_source` to the endpoint and nobody coming to
  this file, and it sat red for a day because the first session to find it
  correctly refused to fix another item's column on its behalf.

  **THE TRAP WAS THE OBVIOUS FIX, AND IT WAS REFUSED.** Changing 31 to 32 makes
  the red go away and teaches the test nothing: **a list edited to match whatever
  the endpoint currently returns can never again report a column appearing or
  disappearing, which is the only thing it exists to do.** So the question asked
  first was not *how do I make this green* but *which of these two is wrong.*

  **THE ENDPOINT IS RIGHT, and it was checked in three places rather than taken
  from its own comment:**
  * `get-booking-receipt/index.ts` names `address_source` in `BOOKING_COLUMNS`
    **on purpose**, in an allow-list whose own header says *"a column added to
    `bookings` tomorrow is private until somebody puts its name here on
    purpose"*;
  * **the customer's own page genuinely draws it** —
    `app/src/book/ManageBookingPage.jsx:438` renders
    `booking.address_source === "typed"` to print *"You typed this address in and
    our lookup had no match for it. If it's right, there's nothing to do."* The
    endpoint's contract is *"every name below is rendered by
    `ManageBookingPage.jsx`"*, and this one is. **A column with no consumer would
    have been the other finding**, and that is what was looked for;
  * **it discloses nothing private.** It is one of two values describing how the
    customer's own address was arrived at, on the customer's own booking, read by
    the customer. `tests/address-source.test.mjs` guards the column's values
    separately, per `CLAUDE.md`.

  **SO THE TEST WAS STALE AND IS NOW CORRECT — 56 passed, 0 failed, exit 0**,
  from 48 passed / 3 failed. The three failures were always one cause: the list
  comparison once, and the per-booking assertion once for each of the two
  bookings it walks.

  **AND THE LIST NOW SAYS WHY IT IS THE LENGTH IT IS**, the way a receipt's floor
  has to say why it is its number:
  * `address_source` carries its own reason where it sits — what draws it, at
    which line, and why its POSITION is not cosmetic (§ 1 compares name for name
    **and in order**, so it sits between `customer_address` and `customer_notes`
    exactly as the endpoint's own array has it);
  * **`EXPECTED_PUBLIC_FIELDS = 32` and `EXPECTED_SHAPE = { BOOKING_COLUMNS: 26,
    EMBEDDED: 3, DERIVED: 3 }` are declared**, with the composition written out:
    26 columns of the row, 3 joined lists (services, add-ons, vehicles), 3 the
    server derives in the business's timezone (booking_date, start_time,
    end_time). **26 + 3 + 3 = 32.** § 1 asserts all four numbers.
  * **So a thirty-third field cannot arrive quietly.** It must be added to the
    endpoint, added here in the right position, rendered by the customer's page
    so § 2 passes, and counted into three declared sizes — four places, two
    languages, two directories. **Two lists agreeing at 33 no longer reads the
    same as two lists agreeing at 32.**

  **BROKEN ON PURPOSE IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, because a guard that only notices
  additions is half a guard:**

  | sabotage | result |
  |---|---|
  | **ADD** a name the endpoint does not return (`internal_flag`) | **5 red** — the declared total, the list comparison, § 2's "nothing renders it", and both per-booking "never arrived" |
  | **REMOVE** a name it does return (`address_source`) | **4 red** — and this reproduces 14.14's original failure exactly, with the declared total now naming it in one line instead of three failures from one cause |
  | **REORDER** — all 32 names present, one in the wrong position | **1 red** |

  **THE THIRD SABOTAGE FOUND A REAL FAULT IN THE CHECK'S OWN MESSAGE.** The
  reorder went red correctly and reported *"endpoint has 32, this file expects
  32: only there [], only here []"* — both counts equal, both set differences
  empty, **because the fault was ORDER and a set difference cannot see order.**
  A check that goes red without saying what is wrong sends the next person
  hunting a missing column that is not missing. It now appends **"first
  difference at position 9: endpoint has \"address_source\", this file has
  \"customer_notes\""**. Found by breaking it, not by reading it.

  Restored after each; `56 passed, 0 failed` at the end, and the canary — a reply
  with `admin_notes` put back — still fires.


### 14.15 — Something refuses `address-suggest` that is not `address-suggest`, and this product cannot see it

- [x] **CLOSED UNREPRODUCED 2026-10-10 — the repro was run and nothing above the function refused; "THE REPRO WAS RUN" at the end of this entry says what was measured and what it does NOT prove.**
  **UNREPRODUCED. Read the last section first — it says what a repro would
  look like, because that is what this item is actually asking somebody for.**
  Found 2026-09-23 while answering the one edge function in 4.4 that was
  refusing for a reason nobody could name. **It is a lead, not a verdict**, and
  it has a line here rather than a mention inside another item because an
  unreproduced finding with no line of its own is exactly how a stale blocker
  survives — this repo watched that cost two days on 2.8.

  **WHAT WAS MEASURED, AND EVERY NUMBER CAME OFF A RUN.**

  - `address-suggest` answered **429 to all six callers** of one replay run —
    owner A, staff A, the removed member, anonymous, and the **service role**.
  - **Its own three rate limits had refused nothing.** `rate_take` counts the
    refused attempt as well as the allowed one, so a refusal made by this
    product appears in the counter. At that moment the counters stood at
    **36 of 60** (per-IP, hourly), **36 of 2,400** (the shared daily address
    budget, keyed on a constant), and **211 of 600** (the blunt public
    ceiling).
  - **The platform logged 82 refusals of that function between 02:16 and
    03:39**, and **none of the 82 is in the counter.** A refusal this
    product's limiter never counted is a refusal this product's limiter never
    made: the function's own code did not get far enough to run.
  - **Geoapify cannot be the source.** The provider seam maps every failure it
    has to `unavailable`, which this function returns as **503**. There is
    exactly one `429` in the whole file and it belongs to the limiter.
  - **It is not latched.** It answered 200 to a single call, to a five-way
    burst, to **18 concurrent real queries**, and to **60 concurrent** cheap
    ones — all after the event.

  **SO THE REFUSAL COMES FROM ABOVE THE FUNCTION. THE THRESHOLD IS NOT NAMED
  HERE, BECAUSE IT COULD NOT BE REPRODUCED ON DEMAND.** That sentence is the
  honest state of this item and it is not to be quietly upgraded by the next
  reader.

  **WHY IT MATTERS EVEN WHILE UNREPRODUCED.** This is the function a customer
  touches on **every keystroke of the address field**. Something refused 82
  calls to it in one evening while the product's own defences sat at 36 of 60.
  **The product's limits for this endpoint are too loose to ever engage
  first**, so whatever is actually refusing is both lower and invisible: when
  it happens the page shows the *"busy, try again"* message that the product's
  own limiter was designed to be the only source of, a detailer's customer
  loses address help, and **nothing anywhere records that it happened.** A
  failure that cannot be counted cannot be noticed, which is this repo's
  oldest shape.

  **WHAT A REPRO WOULD LOOK LIKE, WHICH IS THE ASK.** Not "hit it a lot" —
  that was tried and it answered 200 sixty times at once. What is wanted is a
  run that makes the refusal happen *and* proves who made it:

  1. **Drive it the way the failure did** — from a real browser on the booking
     page's address field, typing, so each keystroke is a separate request
     carrying a CORS preflight. The 82 refusals arrived interleaved with paired
     204s; the harness's own Node calls carry none, which is how the two were
     told apart in the log.
  2. **Read the BODY of the 429, not its status.** This is the whole test. The
     function's own refusal carries `reason: "busy"`. Anything else came from
     above it, and the body is the only thing that distinguishes them — the
     status cannot. The replay now prints A's own response body on every skip
     for exactly this reason.
  3. **Read `rate_hits` immediately before and after.** If the counter did not
     move, the product did not refuse. That single comparison is the finding.
  4. **Then name the ceiling** — concurrency, requests per second, per-function
     or per-project — and write the number down. Until that number exists there
     is nothing to fix, only something to watch.

  **AND THE ONE THING NOT TO DO:** do not loosen or tighten the product's own
  three limits in response to this. They are not what refused, and changing a
  limit that was never consulted would be a change made to a symptom in the
  wrong layer — with the added cost that the shared daily budget is the thing
  standing between one abusive caller and every other detailer's customers
  losing address help until midnight. **CLAUDE.md's rule about a shared
  variable somebody already decided not to change applies here in advance.**

  **SUCCESSOR TO 4.4**, which is ticked. It came out of that item's last
  unexplained refusal and it is the part that outlived it.
  Receipt: `receipts/edge-tenant-replay.json`. See also **14.16**, found in the
  same measurement.

  **Done when** (written 2026-09-25; this item had none): the four steps under
  *"WHAT A REPRO WOULD LOOK LIKE"* have been **run**, and the outcome written here
  **either way** — driven from a real browser's address field so each keystroke
  carries its own preflight; **the BODY of any 429 read rather than its status**,
  because the function's own refusal carries `reason: "busy"` and the status alone
  cannot tell the two apart; `rate_hits` read immediately before and after; and
  **if the counter did not move, the ceiling named with its number.**
  **A run that cannot reproduce it IS a valid close, provided it says so** — this
  item is a lead rather than a verdict, and it says so in its own first line.
  **What failing looks like:** *"unreproduced"* quietly becoming *"fixed"* or
  *"not a problem"*, or somebody changing one of the product's three limits in
  response — **none of which was consulted**, which the entry already warns about
  in advance.

  **THE REPRO WAS RUN — 2026-10-10, `node scripts/address-429-repro.mjs` at
  `ff18202b`. Outcome: NOT REPRODUCED. Nothing above the function refused.**
  Receipt `receipts/address-429-repro.json`: **370 of 370 calls reached**, 10
  assertions, 0 failed. `node scripts/receipt.mjs` grades it valid. All four
  steps, as the done-when asks:

  1. **Driven from a real browser on the booking page.** Bundled Chromium,
     `/book/demo-detail`, at 1440. **What changed since this entry was
     written:** the address box is no longer a per-keystroke type-ahead. Since
     2026-09-13 it has been a **Find button**, one lookup per press
     (`AddressField.jsx` header), so "each keystroke a request" cannot be
     driven any more. The run did two things instead:
     - It pressed the real Find button **70 times**, a different street each
       press.
     - From inside the page it sent **300 calls in three waves of 100 at
       once**, each with a 2-character query. The function refuses those
       **400 before it reaches its limiter**, so they cost nothing, and
       **a 429 there could only come from above the function**.

     The browser sent **107-113 CORS preflights per run**. They were counted
     from Chromium's own network events, because `page.on("response")` does
     not see preflights: the first run counted 0.
  2. **Each 429 was judged by its body.** Burst: **300 of 300 answered 400
     `bad_query`, 0 answered 429**, slowest call 521-736ms over five runs. In
     the receipted run the hour's allowance was already spent, so **all 70
     presses answered 429 and all 70 bodies said `reason: "busy"`**, the
     product's own refusal. The first clean run came before the script was
     committed. Its receipt was overwritten, and it cannot be repeated as it
     was, because it depended on the counter sitting at 36. In that run **24
     presses answered 200, then 46 answered 429, and all 46 bodies said
     `busy`.** **In neither run did a 429 body come from anywhere else.**
  3. **`rate_hits` was read just before and just after the presses.** The
     per-IP counter rose by **70 for 70 presses** in every run, refused ones
     included. The daily counter rose by **24** in the first run, exactly the
     presses that got through, and by **0** in the receipted one. That
     is correct: a caller already over the per-IP limit stops there and is
     never counted against the shared daily budget.
  4. **No ceiling is named, because nothing above the function refused.** The
     counter moved for every refusal.

  **The break, run on purpose:** `--break=blind` makes the script ignore 429
  bodies. That run went **red, 2 failed**: 70 refusals marked "unknown" and
  the product's own refusal not seen
  (`receipts/address-429-repro.sabotage.json`). So the green run really was
  reading the bodies.

  **WHAT THIS DOES NOT PROVE, AND IT MUST NOT BE READ AS "NOT A PROBLEM":**
  it is one IP, one evening, and at most 100 calls at once. A ceiling keyed
  across many IPs, or one that only triggers at higher concurrency, would not
  show up here. **The 82 refusals from 2026-09-23 cannot be re-examined**,
  because the platform logs from that night are gone. The product's three
  limits were **not touched**, as this entry warned in advance.

  **THREE LEADS FROM THIS RUN. They suggest the 82 may have been the product's
  own refusals after all. None of them is a verdict:**
  - **The limiter's hour is a clock hour (`rate_take` uses a fixed window).**
    This run's first attempt started at 19:58 UTC and its 70 presses split
    **34 + 36** across two hours, so the limit never fired. **The 82
    refusals ran 02:16-03:39, which also spans two clock hours**, so a
    reading of one hour's row at "36 of 60" says nothing about refusals
    counted in the hour before.
  - **The per-IP row and the daily row both read 36.** The daily row can
    never be smaller than the sum of all of that day's allowed per-IP calls.
    If the 82 had been product refusals, the previous hour must already have
    allowed 60 calls, so the daily row would have read at least 96. **36 and
    36 agreeing means both rows were created within that hour**, either
    because the day's address traffic really started then, or because the
    rows were deleted.
  - **Something that deletes them existed that evening.**
    `scripts/tabbar-clearance.mjs` deletes every `address%` row from
    `rate_hits` when it starts, including the daily one. Its own header says
    its screen loads exhaust the 60-an-hour allowance "and every load then
    answers 429". Its first commit landed at 20:49 Pacific on 2026-09-23,
    ten minutes after the last of the 82 if those times were UTC. And 14.16
    records another session's browser sweep calling this endpoint at the
    same time.

  Put together: **82 refusals at about one a minute for 83 minutes looks like
  an exhausted hourly allowance, not a burst ceiling**, followed by a
  clearance wiping the evidence. That is the most likely reading, and it is
  **not proven**.

### 14.16 — Two sessions can collide on a public endpoint, and nothing in this repo guards it or reports it

- [x] **Found 2026-09-23, out of a measurement rather than an argument.** The
  edge replay's six calls to `address-suggest` were refused inside a
  three-minute stretch in which the **other session's browser sweep had been
  calling the same endpoint continuously.** Neither session was doing anything
  wrong and neither could see the other.

  **THIS IS A KIND OF COLLISION THIS REPO HAS NEVER WRITTEN DOWN.** Every rule
  we have is about two sessions touching the same FILE — the commit rules, the
  `ROADMAP.md` same-turn rule, the note that `scripts/` is watched by nothing.
  This is two sessions touching the same **running endpoint**, and contending
  for a limit that **lives outside the product entirely**.

  **IT IS WORSE THAN A FILE COLLISION, AND HERE IS THE EXACT REASON.** A file
  collision leaves a diff, or a reload, or a conflict — something changes where
  somebody is looking. This one has **no guard, no report, and no failure.**
  The victim's measurement does not break; **it comes back strange**, and its
  cause is three minutes in the past and in somebody else's pane. On the night
  it was found it cost a wrong entry in `ROADMAP.md` — a function filed as
  refusing for a reason that was never true.

  **THE OPERATING CONSEQUENCE, AND IT IS AN AMENDMENT TO HOW THE LANES ARE KEPT
  APART:** **a lane statement has to say which PUBLIC ENDPOINTS a session is
  going to hit, not only which directories it is going to write.** "I own
  `app/src`" and "I own `scripts/zone-mismatch.mjs`" do not separate two
  sessions that are both about to call `address-suggest`, `create-booking` or
  `available-slots` — and the browser-driven ones call them far harder than a
  script does, because a booking walk types.

  **THE FIRST RULE THAT FALLS OUT OF IT, IN FORCE NOW:** **do not run anything
  that hammers `address-suggest` while another session is in a browser sweep.**
  Stated as a rule rather than a courtesy, by the manager, the night it was
  found.

  **Done when:** the lane-statement shape used at the start of a session names
  endpoints as well as directories, and the shared-resource list is written
  down somewhere a session reads before starting — the address budget, the
  daily email allowance, the demo tenant's rows. **Two of those three have
  already bitten in one night:** this, and the email allowance that the replay
  was silently eating (4.4, round four).

  **SUCCESSOR TO 4.4**, which is ticked. `docs/gotchas.md` carries the
  measurement-level version of this as its own entry.

  **BUILT 2026-09-23. `docs/shared-resources.md`** — one page, deliberately.
  The rule is at the top and the five are each given four lines: what it is in
  plain words, who spends it, what it looks like when somebody spent it first,
  and **whether anything reports the contention**. That last line is the
  useful one, because for four of the five the honest answer is **nothing
  does** — so the page says outright that *the absence of an error is not the
  absence of a collision*.

  The five are what was actually found, not everything imaginable: the booking
  page's **six** public endpoints (read off `app/src/book/` rather than
  guessed — `address-suggest`, `available-slots`, `calculate-booking`,
  `validate-promo-code`, `create-booking`, `track-visit`), the **Geoapify
  budget** at 60 an hour per IP under a 2,400 a day shared cap, the **email
  allowance** at 100 with 80 for tenants, the **demo tenant's rows**, and
  **`rate_hits`** — with `scripts/tabbar-clearance.mjs` named as the one that
  deletes from it.

  **Linked from the two places a session actually looks**: CLAUDE.md, beside
  the `app/src`/`scripts/` collision rules, which now says out loud that every
  rule above it is about files; and `docs/BATCHES.md`, beside the A/B lane
  definition, which now says A and B are about directories and that is not
  enough. **A document nothing points at is a document nobody opens.**

  **NO CHECKER WAS BUILT, AND THAT WAS THE INSTRUCTION.** It is a page a person
  reads. A half-built guard that reported nothing would be worse than an honest
  list, because it would be read as cover. The guard is **14.17**, written down
  and left.

  **Kept honest by its own shape:** the page is one page, and it stays one page.
  If it grows past what somebody will read at dispatch it has failed in the
  same way `docs/README.md` covering 63 of 113 documents has failed.

### 14.18 — A caller with no forwarded-for header is not rate-limited at all

> ## 2026-10-10 — DONE-WHEN ANSWERED: AN OUTSIDE CALLER IS COUNTED, WITH THE HEADER ABSENT AND WITH IT FORGED. THE LIMITS ARE ENFORCED, NOT ADVISORY.
>
> **`node scripts/gateway-header-probe.mjs`, two live calls to `available-slots`
> from this machine, `rate_hits` read (service role, read-only) immediately before
> the first and after each.** Call A sent no `x-forwarded-for`; call B sent
> `x-forwarded-for: 203.0.113.18`, which is not the caller. **A moved one hit on
> `(available-slots, <this machine's real address>)`. B moved one hit on the SAME
> row, and nothing at all landed under 203.0.113.18** — so the gateway writes the
> header itself for an outside caller whether or not they send one, and it
> overwrites a forged one rather than appending to it (an appended value would
> have put the forged address left-most and the row under it). Both calls answered
> 200. Run twice with the script at its final commit (`86f634a3`): identical both
> times; the receipt is `receipts/gateway-header-probe.json` (valid, 2/2 targets,
> 5 assertions, canary seen).
>
> **The reader was proven before its silence could mean anything:** the script
> writes a control row through `rate_take`, must read it back, deletes it, and
> makes NO public call if it cannot. `--break=blind` (reader pointed at the wrong
> bucket) goes red as UNJUDGEABLE with zero calls. `--break=blind-calls` (control
> passes, the reads around the two calls are blinded) makes the same two calls
> report *"NOT COUNTED ... per-IP limits are advisory"*, so the check can come out
> the other way. Only the last sabotage's receipt is on disk
> (`receipts/gateway-header-probe.sabotage.json`, `--break=blind`); the
> `blind-calls` verdict is quoted from its run, not kept.
>
> **What this does NOT show, stated so a sweep does not "find" it:** one machine,
> one function, one evening, and `cf-connecting-ip` was not forged (`ipOf` only
> reads it when `x-forwarded-for` is blank, which the gateway never leaves blank
> for an outside caller). A caller who arrives header-less from INSIDE the project
> (`pg_net`, the 6.2 probe) is still uncounted on the code that is RUNNING —
> `_shared/rateLimit.ts` is fixed in source (2026-10-06 below) and not published,
> and publishing is Andrew's. So the fix is now insurance against an inside caller
> and a gateway that one day stops writing the header, not a hole an outsider was
> using. **14.15's unnamed ceiling is therefore NOT explained by this**: our
> limiter does count an outside caller, as the item feared it might not.

- [x] **Found 2026-09-23 by an absence, while building 6.2's outside checks.**
  The new monitor called `available-slots` about eight times through `pg_net`.
  `available-slots` is rate-limited on `LIMITS.publicCeiling` keyed by
  `ipOf(req)`, and `rate_take` counts the refused attempt as well as the
  allowed one — so eight calls should have left a row. **`rate_hits` has no
  row for that bucket at all.**

  **The mechanism is in the open and is deliberate as far as it goes.**
  `ipOf` reads `x-forwarded-for` and falls back to `cf-connecting-ip`;
  `pg_net` sets neither, so the key is blank, and `rate_take`'s first branch
  says so in its own comment: *"NOTHING TO COUNT AGAINST IS NOT THE SAME AS
  BEING OVER THE LIMIT. A missing forwarded-for header must not lock out a
  real customer."* That reasoning is right about a real customer behind a
  proxy that drops a header. **The consequence nobody has written down is the
  other half: a caller who can arrive without that header is not counted, and
  therefore has no ceiling.**

  **THIS IS CONVENIENT FOR 6.2 AND THAT IS EXACTLY WHY IT IS WRITTEN DOWN
  RATHER THAN ENJOYED.** It is the reason the monitor cannot exhaust a
  session's bucket or be throttled by one, which is a real benefit — and
  taking only the convenient half of a measurement is how a finding
  disappears.

  **WHAT IS NOT KNOWN, AND THE ITEM DOES NOT PRETEND OTHERWISE:** whether a
  caller from the public internet can reach these functions without that
  header. Supabase's edge almost certainly sets it on the way in, which would
  make this harmless and internal-only. **That was not tested** — testing it
  means probing the live gateway's header handling, and the session that found
  it was told not to hammer public endpoints.

  **What a check would look like:** call one rate-limited public function from
  outside with the header absent, and with it forged to a value that is not
  the caller, and read `rate_hits` after each. If either leaves no row, the
  per-IP limits are advisory rather than enforced and **14.15's unnamed
  ceiling is doing more work than this product's own limits are.** Sibling to
  14.15, which is the same shape seen from the other side: something refusing
  that our limiter never counted, and now our limiter not counting at all.

  **Done when** (written 2026-09-25; this item had none): one rate-limited public
  function has been called from outside **with `x-forwarded-for` absent**, and
  again **with it forged to a value that is not the caller**, and `rate_hits` read
  immediately after each — **with the answer written here either way.**
  **If either call leaves no row, the per-IP limits are advisory rather than
  enforced. That is the finding, not a failure of the test**, and it closes this
  item as much as a clean result would.
  **What failing looks like:** a conclusion of *"Supabase's edge probably sets the
  header"* with no counter read — which is exactly what this entry already says it
  does not know.
  **Whose job / what it costs:** it means probing the live gateway, and the
  session that found this was told not to hammer public endpoints. **Two calls,
  not a loop** — it needs somebody holding permission to touch a public endpoint,
  not a load test.

  > ## 2026-10-06 — FIX BUILT AND LOOP-PROVED IN SOURCE. NOT DEPLOYED, AND THE
  > ITEM'S OWN DONE-WHEN (THE TWO OUTSIDE CALLS) IS STILL UNANSWERED.
  >
  > **DP Cowork2. The change is one file, `supabase/functions/_shared/rateLimit.ts`,
  > and no migration.** `ipOf` used to answer a blank string when neither header
  > was there, and the blank was skipped **twice** — by `withinLimits`
  > (`if (!l.key) continue`) and again by `rate_take`'s first branch. Now:
  >
  > - `ipOf` never answers blank. With no header it answers `NO_ADDRESS`
  >   (`"no-address"`, not an IP and not mistakable for one).
  > - `withinLimits` sends every limit keyed on `NO_ADDRESS` to **one shared
  >   counter per bucket**, `<bucket>:no-address` / key `all`, with
  >   `LIMITS.noAddress` = **3,000 an hour** instead of the per-IP number.
  > - **A blank key that is not an address (a phone, an email nobody gave) is
  >   still skipped** — there is nothing to count. `rate_take`'s blank branch is
  >   untouched, because the migration is append-only and it still serves those.
  >
  > **All 18 callers pick it up with no edit** — every use is
  > `key: ipOf(req)` (`grep -rn "ipOf(req)" supabase/functions`); the one that
  > assigns it to a variable, `address-suggest`, only passes it into limit keys.
  >
  > **WHY THIS SHAPE, WHEN THE BRIEF SUGGESTED A SEPARATE SHARED BUCKET WITH A
  > GENEROUS CEILING AND THAT IS WHAT IT IS.** Two cheaper-looking options lose:
  > (1) *return a constant from `ipOf` and stop* — then every header-less caller
  > shares the per-IP numbers, which are sized for one person (`plan-link`: 6 an

  > (2) *make `rate_take` count blank keys* — needs a migration Andrew applies,
  > and counts blank phones and emails too, which are not callers. **Why 3,000:**
  > it is one row for everybody who arrives this way, so it has to cover the
  > sum, not a person; the only traffic known to arrive without an address is the
  > five-minute `probe-live-site` job (`*/5 * * * *` in
  > `20260923040000_outside_checks.sql`: 12 an hour, `available-slots` only), so
  > it is about 250 times that; and the worst a script gets is 3,000 invocations
  > an hour per function, which is cents. **What it does not claim:** if an
  > outsider CAN arrive header-less, they can pin that one counter and the probe
  > behind it would be refused. That is the next half and it is not measured.
  >
  > **PROVED BY RUNNING IT** — `node tests/rate-limit-loops.test.mjs`, section 3,

### 14.19 — A two-car booking's stored `subtotal` counts the second car twice, and nobody has ever been in a position to notice

- [x] **FIXED 2026-09-23. One line in `_shared/pricing.ts`, and the located
  change was one line away from where the fault actually lived.**

  **THE ENTRY SAID `pricing.ts:655`. THAT LINE WAS ALREADY CORRECT.** 655 is
  `subtotalBase = beforeAdjustments + adjustmentsTotal`, and the
  `adjustmentsTotal` in scope there is `rulesTotal + planLine` — rules and
  plan only, with the extra cars deliberately left out because
  `beforeAdjustments` already holds them. Its own comment says so: *"the extra
  cars are DRAWN with the adjustments and are already COUNTED in
  `beforeAdjustments`, so they lead the list and stay out of the total
  below. Counting them twice would double the price of the second car, which
  is the shape of defect this file exists to prevent."* **That warning was
  written, was correct, and was obeyed — sixty lines further down, by a
  different piece of code, it was not.**

  The fault is at **line 715**, added by ROADMAP 2.2's rounding fold:

  ```
  const adjustmentsTotalFinal = adjustmentLines.reduce((s, l) => s + l.amount, 0);
  const subtotalBaseFinal = beforeAdjustments + adjustmentsTotalFinal;   // ← extras counted twice
  ```

  2.2 recomputes the totals after folding a rounding gap into the last
  discount line, and it recomputes them **from the array**, which contains the
  extra-vehicle lines. So the same figure `beforeAdjustments` already held was
  added a second time. **The fix is `- extrasTotal` on that line**, with the
  reason recorded above it.

  **AND THE NAME IS THE WHOLE TRAP: `adjustmentsTotal` MEANS TWO DIFFERENT
  THINGS SIXTY LINES APART, AND BOTH ARE RIGHT.** The local one excludes the
  cars because the cars are already in the base. The **returned** one includes
  them, because `StepReview.jsx` and `tests/pricing-lines-sum.test.mjs` both
  sum the lines a customer is *shown*, and `basePrice` describes one car — so
  a returned figure without the cars would break the line-sum everywhere else.
  Neither value is wrong; adding the second to `beforeAdjustments` is. The
  returned field is left exactly as it was.

  **2.2 IS NOT AT FAULT AND ITS FIX STAYS.** The fold was correct when it was
  written — multi-car did not reach a single tenant until 2026-09-21, so
  `extraLines` was empty for every booking in existence and `adjustmentsTotal`
  and `adjustmentsTotalFinal` were the same number. **8.10 then put entries
  into that array, and the recompute quietly changed meaning without changing
  a character.** A one-car booking is byte-for-byte unchanged by this fix.

  **CONFIRMED BY RE-RENDERING THE EMAIL, NOT BY REASONING.** The real
  `customerConfirmationEmail` with engine-produced numbers, the item's own
  scenario, before and after:

  ```
  BEFORE (subtotal 315)              AFTER (subtotal 215)
  shape service            $215      shape service            $115
  2nd vehicle · Small      $100      2nd vehicle · Small      $100
  Discount applied        -$100      Estimated total          $215
  Estimated total          $215
  ```

  The `Discount applied` line is gone because there is no longer a gap for
  `reconcile()` to close. **`emailTemplates.ts` was not touched**, as the
  verdict required.

  **THE CHECK THAT NOW EXISTS: `tests/quoted-lines-true.test.mjs`.**
  Credential-free, no dev server, no deploy — 14 tests. It runs the real
  `computeQuote`, builds the payload `create-booking/index.ts:650-676` builds,
  renders the real customer confirmation and **reads the money column out of
  the rendered HTML**.

  **It asks the question the existing checks do not.** `quoteLines()` never
  receives a service price — it DERIVES one, `subtotal + siteDiscount −
  travel − Σ(lines)`, and prints the answer to a paying customer. So the
  stored `subtotal` is not a display figure; it is the input to a subtraction.
  The property asserted is that the derived figure equals what the customer
  was actually quoted for the work — `basePrice + sizeAdd + addOnsTotal`.
  That identity survives travel, surcharges, plans, site sales, promo codes
  and rounding, and it failed on exactly one path. **The old sum is asserted
  too, in the same test**, because a check that only asked the new half could
  be satisfied by deleting every number.

  **BROKEN ON PURPOSE, TWICE, BEFORE BEING BELIEVED.**
  - Reintroducing the fault (`- extrasTotal` removed): **one car stays green,
    all eleven multi-car scenarios go red**, plus the "invents no discount"
    test. That is the important one — the fault *balances*, and this is the
    first check in the repo that sees through a balanced column.
  - Understating the subtotal by **one dollar**: all fourteen go red,
    including the one-car control. A $1 error anywhere is caught.
  Both reverted; 14/14 green at the committed state.

  **WHAT THE EXISTING CHECKS SAID WHILE THE FAULT WAS LIVE**, measured rather
  than assumed: `tests/pricing-lines-sum.test.mjs` 14/14, `multi-vehicle`
  63/0 (its item 2d is that same sum by hand),
  `render-emails.mjs`'s money-column assertion clean. **None of them was
  wrong. They were all asking whether it adds up.**

  **AND `render-emails.mjs`'S OWN FIXTURE COULD NEVER HAVE CAUGHT IT.**
  `carloadBooking` is hand-written with `subtotal: 480, total: 480` — the

  **STILL NOT LIVE, AND THAT IS ANDREW'S CALL, NOT A SESSION'S.**

  **NOT COVERED, SAID PLAINLY:** `splitDays`. Cars on different days are

  - **The invoice's `Booking total` was a third copy of `345`.** It is

  **PROVED BY BREAKING THE ENGINE TWICE AND COUNTING WHAT MOVED — and the
  count corrected a premise this item was working from.** It was assumed
  that *"thirty of the thirty-two emails ride on those two bases"* and would

  - **A stored-`subtotal` fault moves 5** — the three confirmations, the

  - **A `total` fault moves 16** — adding the invoice, the receipt, the

  - **`render-emails.mjs` itself reported PASS under both faults.**
